desc:
An IPv4 address in dotted-decimal notation is written as four octets separated by single dots, such as 192.168.0.1. Return true if the string s is a valid address, otherwise false.

The rules are:

  • there are exactly four octets, separated by exactly three . characters;
  • each octet is a non-empty sequence of the decimal digits 0-9 only (no signs, no letters);
  • an octet has no leading zero unless it is the single digit 0;
  • the numeric value of each octet is at most 255.

For example, 192.168.0.1 and 0.0.0.0 are valid. 256.1.1.1 (too large), 1.01.1.1 (leading zero), 1.1.1 (three octets) and 1.-1.1.1 (a sign) are not.
constraints: s contains digits, letters, and the characters . + -; it has no spaces
hints: Split the string on . and look at the pieces. How many pieces must there be?
Check each piece separately: non-empty, only digits, at most 3 characters, no leading zero unless it is exactly 0, then its value.
Be careful with strings like 1..1.1 or 1.1.1. (empty pieces after splitting) and with +1 or -0 (a sign is not a digit, so do not rely on a library integer parser alone).
editorial: The format is local to each octet, so split on dots and validate the pieces independently. The split must give exactly four pieces; this also rejects too few or too many dots, and leading, trailing or doubled dots because those create empty pieces.

For a piece, first reject it if it is empty or longer than three characters, then reject any character outside 0-9, then reject a leading zero when the length is more than one, and finally compare the numeric value with 255. Checking the characters yourself matters: library parsers such as int() accept a sign and surrounding spaces, which this format forbids.
Every piece is looked at once and has at most three characters, so the work is linear in the length of s.
